**Defeating Marine Le Pen (2017 and 2022)**
Macron beat far-right leader Marine Le Pen in the runoffs of two French presidential elections. In May 2017 he won about 66 percent of the vote against her as the National Front candidate, and in the 2022 rematch he defeated her again, by then leading the renamed National Rally, to win a second term.

**En Marche! and Renaissance**
The centrist political movement Macron founded in April 2016, whose initials match his own. It was renamed La République En Marche! after his 2017 victory and Renaissance in 2022, and it leads the centrist Ensemble coalition in Parliament.

**2023 pension reform, Article 49.3, and Élisabeth Borne**
In March 2023, Macron's government raised the retirement age from 62 to 64 by using Article 49.3 of the French Constitution, which lets the government pass a bill without a vote in the National Assembly. The move sparked mass strikes and protests, and the government of Prime Minister Élisabeth Borne, only the second woman to hold the post, narrowly survived the resulting no-confidence votes.

**Yellow Vest protests (gilets jaunes)**
A protest movement that began in November 2018 against a planned fuel tax increase and broadened into anger over the cost of living and Macron's perceived elitism. Protesters wearing the yellow high-visibility vests French drivers must carry occupied traffic roundabouts across France, and some protests in Paris turned violent.

**2019–2020 pension strikes**
Macron's first-term plan to merge France's 42 separate pension systems into a single points-based system triggered one of the longest transportation strikes in modern French history, organized by unions including the CGT. The plan was suspended in 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic.

**"Jupiterian" president**
Macron said he wanted to be a "Jupiterian" president, comparing himself to Jupiter, the king of the Roman gods, who stays above the everyday fray. Critics used the label to attack him as aloof and arrogant; his 2017 official portrait notably included two smartphones on his desk.

**Rothschild banker and the Nestlé–Pfizer deal**
After graduating from the elite ENA school and working as a civil servant, Macron became an investment banker at Rothschild & Co. He made his fortune by leading Nestlé's 2012 purchase of Pfizer's baby-food business, a deal worth about $12 billion.

**Minister of Economy under François Hollande**
Macron served as Minister of the Economy, Industry and Digital Affairs from 2014 in the Socialist government of Prime Minister Manuel Valls under President François Hollande. He resigned in 2016 to launch his own presidential campaign.

**Benalla affair**
A 2018 scandal involving Alexandre Benalla, a security aide to Macron who was filmed beating protesters while wearing a police helmet at a May Day demonstration in Paris. The revelation that he had been only lightly punished caused Macron's approval ratings to drop.

**Great National Debate and closing the ENA**
In response to the Yellow Vest protests, Macron launched the "great national debate" in 2019, a series of town halls and public consultations across France. He later announced the closure of the École nationale d'administration (ENA), the elite civil service school he had attended, replacing it with a new institute.

**Samuel Paty and French secularism**
Samuel Paty was a schoolteacher beheaded near Paris in October 2020 after showing his students caricatures of the Prophet Muhammad during a class on free speech. Macron defended secularism (laïcité) and the right to publish the cartoons, prompting protests and boycotts in some Muslim-majority countries.

**AUKUS submarine dispute**
In September 2021, Australia canceled a multibillion-dollar deal to buy French submarines in favor of nuclear-powered submarines under the new AUKUS pact with the United States and United Kingdom. France responded by recalling its ambassadors to the U.S. and Australia.

**"We must not humiliate Russia"**
A 2022 remark by Macron arguing that Russia should not be humiliated so that a diplomatic exit from the war in Ukraine would remain possible. Ukrainian officials and other critics condemned the statement.

**Hoodie war-room photos**
In March 2022, early in the Russian invasion of Ukraine, official photos showed an unshaven Macron in jeans and a hoodie in the Élysée Palace. Critics mocked them as an attempt to imitate Volodymyr Zelenskyy's wartime look.

**Brigitte Macron's official status**
In 2017, Macron faced backlash, including a petition, over plans to create an official "first lady" role for his wife Brigitte, his former high school teacher. The plan came while he was pushing a law to "moralize" politics, including banning lawmakers from employing family members, and he settled for a transparency charter instead.
